summary: This Wikipedia article explains passive solar building design, an architectural approach in which windows, walls, and floors collect, store, reflect, and distribute solar heat without mechanical or electrical systems. It covers passive solar technologies, the scientific basis drawn from climatology, thermodynamics and heat transfer, the role of sun path and latitude in design, heat transfer principles, site considerations, and design elements and pitfalls for temperate residential buildings. The note is partly cut off before its final section on efficiency.
one_line: Overview of passive solar building design, which uses windows, walls, floors and thermal mass to collect and store solar heat without mechanical systems.
key_facts: In passive solar building design, windows, walls, and floors are made to collect, store, reflect, and distribute solar energy in the form of heat in the winter and reject solar heat in the summer.
Passive solar design is called passive because, unlike active solar heating systems, it does not involve the use of mechanical and electrical devices.
The key to designing a passive solar building is to best take advantage of the local climate by performing an accurate site analysis.
Passive solar design techniques can be applied most easily to new buildings, but existing buildings can be adapted or retrofitted.
A common example of passive solar technology is a solarium on the equator-side of a building.

Passive solar technologies include direct and indirect solar gain for space heating, solar water heating systems based on the thermosiphon, thermal mass, solar cookers, the solar chimney, and earth sheltering.
The 47-degree difference in the altitude of the sun at solar noon between winter and summer forms the basis of passive solar design.
Uncontrolled air infiltration from poor weatherization can contribute up to 40% of heat loss during winter.
Roofs receive the majority of the solar radiation delivered to a house.
External shading is more effective at reducing heat gain than internal window coverings.
A common recommendation for residential dwellings is to place living areas facing solar noon and sleeping quarters on the opposite side.
A heliodon is a traditional movable light device used by architects and designers to help model sun path effects.

The article states that if passive solar design had been applied comprehensively to new building construction beginning in 1980, the United States could be saving over $250,000,000 per year on energy and related pollution today.
Thermography with digital thermal imaging cameras has been one of the most useful post-construction evaluation tools for a formal quantitative energy audit.
Excessive glass area ('over-glazing') can result in overheating, glare, fading of soft furnishings, and heat loss when ambient air temperatures fall.
